{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_017dsx1nQN6bUYAeENdzn4Q5","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n90\t  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n91\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"2ec75296-8d8c-439e-8f8a-32450f75597d","uuid":"b9bf382d-bcca-488a-ac93-ce8a094e6bd0","timestamp":"2026-10-02T23:54:19.051Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-models\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_gooj754f37w7spymgtmprhbqgxur5trof2ypeg6xhrq4taclypya","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Autonomous GitHub issue triage and resolution agent\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** An agent that reads new GitHub issues, labels them, flags duplicates, and asks for missing info. For issues a maintainer opts in, it drafts a fix as a pull request (PR) that a human reviews and merges.\n- **Type:** AI-agentic plus software. The agent is greenfield, but it attaches to existing repos and CI (brownfield-lite). Humans doing triage today is the fallback path. This is not a small build: outside users author the input, it spends money, and it acts on code.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness and security (containment of untrusted input).\n- **Worst failure:** Attacker-authored issue text, comments, or repo content steers the agent into leaking secrets or private code, or into landing malicious code on a protected branch. V2 and V3 guard this, and human-only merge enforced by GitHub branch protection backs them up.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Webhook acknowledgment | Respond within GitHub's webhook timeout, then process async | REQUIREMENT (GitHub webhook docs) | V0 |\n| Triage latency | p95 ≤ 5 min from issue opened to proposal | ASSUMPTION (typical \"fast first response\" goal; owner to confirm) | V4 |\n| Throughput | Pilot repo only, low volume; real rate UNKNOWN (see Missing inputs) | UNKNOWN | V0 baseline |\n| Availability / SLO | Best effort. If the agent is down, issues still work and humans triage. | ASSUMPTION (agent is additive) | Phase 0 alert |\n| RPO / RTO | GitHub is the system of record. Agent DB holds run state and audit log, rebuildable from GitHub. RPO is N/A for state. The audit log is retained per org policy (UNKNOWN). | ASSUMPTION | Phase 1 |\n| AI inference cost | Hard cap during the pilot: $20/day for the whole org (basis: one repo, a kill switch). Per triaged issue ≤ $0.10. Per accepted draft PR ≤ $5. | ASSUMPTION | V0 (cap), V4, V5 |\n| Resource use | Sandbox: ≤ 15 min wall-clock and ≤ 4 vCPU per run | ASSUMPTION (design parameter, tune in V5) | V3, V5 |\n| Operational complexity | ≤ 3 deployables (webhook API, worker, sandbox runner) plus Postgres and a queue | ASSUMPTION | Phase 4 review |\n\n**Missing inputs** (none changes the phase order, so I'm proceeding on the assumptions below):\n- **Repo scope:** Assumed one pilot repo with CI and reasonable tests, where public or external users can file issues. If none has tests, Phase 3 resolution moves to deferred. The owner supplies this before Phase 0.\n- **Model provider and data terms:** Assumed a hosted provider under enterprise no-training, zero-retention terms (see V1). The security or legal owner supplies this before Phase 0.\n- **Numbers:** Issue volume, the monthly budget, and maintainers' review-time tolerance are needed before the Phase 0 cap and V5. The engineering owner supplies them.\n- **GitHub org admin:** An admin must approve the GitHub App install. Request this first because it has lead time.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| GitHub App install on the pilot repo | Org admin approval | organizational (ASSUMED) | deployed |\n| Any repo text sent to the model API | V1: data-egress sign-off | risk/security + organizational | exposed |\n| Every write to GitHub beyond dry run | V2: injection containment | risk/security | exposed |\n| Executing repo code or tests | V3: sandbox isolation | risk/security | deployed |\n| Triage auto-apply (no per-item approval) | V4: label and duplicate quality | validation | hardened |\n| Resolution loop design | V4: retrieval finds the relevant code and issues | validation | specified |\n| Eval sets (≈200 labeled historical issues; ≈30 closed issues with known fixes and tests) | Maintainer time | organizational | V4 and V5 run |\n| Widening to more repos or external-author issues | V5: cost per accepted PR, reviewer burden | economic + validation | scaled |\n| Daily cost cap value | Budget owner | organizational | V0 passing |\n\nNo decision dependency binds beyond §3. All structural and runtime dependencies are shown by the phase order.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Autonomy and trust boundary | R3 (trust boundary; a bad merge is harm that can't be undone) | The agent only comments, labels, and opens draft PRs on `agent/*` branches. A human merges. Branch protection, CODEOWNERS, and required CI are enforced by GitHub, not by the agent. The agent cannot touch `.github/`, lockfiles, or secrets paths. | Maintainer review is affordable | V2, V3 | Auto-merge is considered only after V5 plus months of measured history. See §10. |\n| Data-privacy boundary and hosting (hosted API vs self-host) | R3 (code leaves the org; data gravity at a vendor) | Hosted model API under zero-retention enterprise terms. Pilot repo contents only, no secrets. | The security owner accepts the terms | V1 | V1 fails, or the repo is classified too sensitive. Then self-host or restrict to issue text only. |\n| Execution isolation | R3 (trust boundary; untrusted code runs) | Ephemeral microVM or gVisor container per run. Egress only through an allow-listed package proxy. No agent or GitHub credentials inside. Repo mounted in and the diff returned out. | Isolation holds against malicious repo content | V3 | V3 fails. Then no code execution and triage only. |\n| Identity and hosting | R2 (permission changes need org re-approval per repo) | A GitHub App with least privilege: issues write, pull requests write, contents write limited to `agent/*` branches, metadata read. No PATs and no Actions-with-secrets. The service runs outside the repo's CI. | Those permissions suffice | Phase 0 permission review (named reviewer, pass/fail) | The App can't be scoped to a branch prefix. Then use a bot fork for PRs. |\n| Prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | R2 | Prompt plus retrieval (issue history, code search). No fine-tuning. Never train on repo or user data (R3). | Retrieval closes the quality gap | V4 | V4 fails after retrieval tuning and enough reviewed labels exist. Revisit with a privacy review. |\n| Eligibility to resolve | R2 (changes the workflow of maintainers and contributors) | Resolution runs only on issues a maintainer labels `agent-ok`. An issue's author can't trigger code execution. | Opt-in is acceptable to maintainers | V2 | Maintainers want wider triggers. Re-run V2 with the new trigger. |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- **Monolith vs services:** modular monolith (API, worker) plus a separate sandbox runner.\n- **Sync vs async:** acknowledge the webhook, enqueue, and process async with idempotency keys on the delivery ID (at-least-once, duplicate-safe writes).\n- **Consistency vs availability:** favor availability, since GitHub is the source of truth and the agent is additive.\n- **State store:** Postgres plus a queue (SQS or Redis).\n- **Build vs buy:** build on an agent SDK. Spend one day comparing against an off-the-shelf coding agent. If one meets V4 and V5 thresholds inside V1–V3 constraints, buy instead.\n\n**N/A:** Brownfield migration, cutover, and system-of-record transfer. Nothing is migrated, and GitHub stays the system of record.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request:** A real issue opened by a maintainer on the allow-listed pilot repo. GitHub sends a webhook (signature verified) to the API, which enqueues it. The worker fetches the issue and calls the model with issue text wrapped as untrusted data. The model returns a structured triage proposal (label, duplicate candidates, missing-info question). The agent writes the proposal to the trace and an internal channel (dry run) and performs no GitHub write.\n- **Tiers:** GitHub → webhook API → queue → worker → model API → Postgres audit log → internal channel.\n- **Deploy and rollback:** The pipeline builds a container image and deploys from IaC (Terraform). Rollback redeploys the previous image. A feature flag or kill switch disables the agent without a deploy. Both are exercised once.\n- **Logging and monitoring:** OpenTelemetry trace per issue from webhook to model call. Structured logs with issue text redacted or classified like the repo data. Metrics for tokens, cost, latency, and errors. Alerts on queue age, error rate, and the daily cost cap.\n- **Hard caps:** Per-run token cap and the $20/day org cap (ASSUMPTION, §1). The cap is enforced in the model-access seam, which cuts off runs.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only the allow-listed pilot repo, with maintainer-authored issues, behind the flag. Nothing is written back and no code is executed. Repo content leaves the org only after V1.\n\n**Exit check (V0):** A real issue yields one trace across every tier. A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline. An injected failure (model API down, or the cap breached) fires an alert. Baseline floor values are recorded for latency, cost per issue, and queue delay.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Guardrails before capability**\n  - Unlocks: Any write to GitHub, any code execution, and non-maintainer input.\n  - Depends on: Phase 0 and V1.\n  - Tasks, widest blast radius first:\n    1. Tool executor with a tool allow-list and argument validation.\n    2. Approval binding: a write runs only with an approval bound to that exact action. The executor enforces it, not the model, and logs it.\n    3. Author trust tiers (maintainer, member, external), with untrusted content fenced as data.\n    4. No outbound URLs, images, or other egress from model output.\n    5. Sandbox runner (V3).\n    6. Injection suite in CI (V2).\n    7. Per-run iteration limits and a per-repo kill switch.\n  - Rollback: Flip the flag to dry run. The executor denies all writes by default.\n  - Exit check: V2 and V3 pass.\n\n- **Phase 2: Triage (retrieval, model access, run state)**\n  - Unlocks: Live labels and comments on the pilot repo, then external-author issues.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, and the triage eval set from maintainers.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** An agent that reads new GitHub issues, labels them, flags duplicates, and asks for missing info. For issues a maintainer opts in, it drafts a fix as a pull request (PR) that a human reviews and merges.\n- **Type:** AI-agentic plus software. The agent is greenfield, but it attaches to existing repos and CI (brownfield-lite). Humans doing triage today is the fallback path. This is not a small build: outside users author the input, it spends money, and it acts on code.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness and security (containment of untrusted input).\n- **Worst failure:** Attacker-authored issue text, comments, or repo content steers the agent into leaking secrets or private code, or into landing malicious code on a protected branch. V2 and V3 guard this, and human-only merge enforced by GitHub branch protection backs them up.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Webhook acknowledgment | Respond within GitHub's webhook timeout, then process async | REQUIREMENT (GitHub webhook docs) | V0 |\n| Triage latency | p95 ≤ 5 min from issue opened to proposal | ASSUMPTION (typical \"fast first response\" goal; owner to confirm) | V4 |\n| Throughput | Pilot repo only, low volume; real rate UNKNOWN (see Missing inputs) | UNKNOWN | V0 baseline |\n| Availability / SLO | Best effort. If the agent is down, issues still work and humans triage. | ASSUMPTION (agent is additive) | Phase 0 alert |\n| RPO / RTO | GitHub is the system of record. Agent DB holds run state and audit log, rebuildable from GitHub. RPO is N/A for state. The audit log is retained per org policy (UNKNOWN). | ASSUMPTION | Phase 1 |\n| AI inference cost | Hard cap during the pilot: $20/day for the whole org (basis: one repo, a kill switch). Per triaged issue ≤ $0.10. Per accepted draft PR ≤ $5. | ASSUMPTION | V0 (cap), V4, V5 |\n| Resource use | Sandbox: ≤ 15 min wall-clock and ≤ 4 vCPU per run | ASSUMPTION (design parameter, tune in V5) | V3, V5 |\n| Operational complexity | ≤ 3 deployables (webhook API, worker, sandbox runner) plus Postgres and a queue | ASSUMPTION | Phase 4 review |\n\n**Missing inputs** (none changes the phase order, so I'm proceeding on the assumptions below):\n- **Repo scope:** Assumed one pilot repo with CI and reasonable tests, where public or external users can file issues. If none has tests, Phase 3 resolution moves to deferred. The owner supplies this before Phase 0.\n- **Model provider and data terms:** Assumed a hosted provider under enterprise no-training, zero-retention terms (see V1). GitHub sends a webhook (signature verified) to the API, which enqueues it. The worker fetches the issue and calls the model with issue text wrapped as untrusted data. Deliberately deferred\n- **Auto-merge of agent PRs:** pulled forward only after a sustained V5 history, an explicit risk acceptance by the repo owner, and a fresh V2/V3 run.\n- **Auto-closing duplicates or stale issues:** pulled forward when duplicate precision has held above the V4 bar on live data and closing can be undone.\n- **Security-vulnerability reports and private advisories:** excluded from scope.
